paragraphs.text: Beautiful are the meadows of piety. They are not bright with colours that fade; they teem with heavenly flowers. The flowers of piety are the fruits of a godly way of life. For the virtues lead us up to that wonderful, original beauty which was made in the image and likeness of God. This likeness that comes through virtue does not allow a man to be called a horse instead of a man. So when we pursue it, we are no longer named wolf and dragon and snake and scorpion, sinking down to the degradation of the irrational animals. Instead we are, and are called, and are believed to be a wonderful and honoured image of God, one that keeps the original beauty of its stamp. You were made master of the irrational animals, so do not imitate the habits of your servants. This is not because the irrational animals are bad, for nothing evil was created by the Good One. Let no one suppose that the irrational animals are ranked as evil because they are brought forward as an image of the evil of those who do not live by virtue. If that were so, how could Scripture say, "And God saw all that he had made, and behold, it was good" – and not simply good, but "very good"? Someone may say: created things are brought forward as images of evil, for the lion is an image of the tyrant, the serpent of the man who is crooked and utterly wicked in character, the scorpion of the violent man, and the wolf of the rapacious one. So how could created things be good when they are so plainly taken as images of evil? Those who love learning must understand that these traits neither are nor are called evil in their own nature; they are a condition proper to irrational animals. But when such a condition passes into the rational nature, it disgraces the sight and dulls rational freedom. You have received, O man, the rank of master; do not pursue the dishonourable and servile station of the irrational animals. You disgrace yourself by imitating the beastliness of the irrational animals. This is not because the animals are evil or are called evil, but because a dishonourable and servile image does not suit the free. Suppose a distinguished and renowned man puts on or wraps himself in a slave's garment. He is disgraced and shamed, not because the clothing is poor and filthy, but because it suits a slave and does not befit a free man. In the same way, if you take on the character of a scorpion or a wolf, it is not the nature of the irrational animals that is maligned. It is your own condition that is disgraced, for it was allotted mastery and yet pursues the things of a slave. I have had to say this, so that no one takes what has been said as an insult to creation, as if God had made something bad. All things are truly "good" and "very good," if they keep their proper order and follow their proper law. And so that you may learn, beloved, that nothing was made bad by nature by God, God has taught us to take an image even from these irrational animals. He has set before us certain excellences of the irrational animals to imitate, so that we may not slander created things as evil. We are to imitate not their nature as a whole, but whatever befits a rational condition. Or did you not hear the author of Proverbs saying today, "Go to the ant, you sluggard, and emulate its ways"? Did you not understand how, by setting before us the industry of the ant, he trained us towards tireless zeal? Did we not teach you plainly to learn tirelessness from the ant and skill from the bee? For it is possible, truly possible, as I said before, to gather like flowers certain excellences even of the irrational animals that befit a rational condition. Yet these things are said to our shame and reproach. Since you did not imitate God, he says, imitate the ant. Have you never seen a true father rebuke his children and, after much correction, point them to the servants as an example? He says plainly: "Imitate at least the servant, who is beneath you in rank but surpasses you in skill." So the God who loves mankind exposes our senselessness: he brings forward the ant to reprove our sloth and the bee to reprove our laziness. It is clear from this that nothing evil was made by God. Rather, he gave you perception and a discerning mind, so that you might flee the habits of the irrational animals and seize their excellences. Even the lion can be an image of virtue, when you take the image to mean not tyranny but courage; for tyranny is one thing and courage another. That is why Scripture, announcing the good news of the Saviour who was to rise from Judah, says: "Judah is a lion's whelp; from a shoot, my son, you have gone up; you lay down and slept like a lion, and like a whelp." See how great a likeness the divine word builds from the excellences found in the irrational animals. It is possible, then, to imitate a lion with understanding. It is also possible to imitate the serpent, not by spitting venom but by acquiring its shrewdness, as the Saviour also says to the apostles: "Be shrewd as the serpent." If the creature were bad, he would not have called his own image to imitate what is bad by saying, "Be shrewd as the serpent." Imitate in the serpent not its venom, not its rage, but its shrewdness. If you imitate its venom, David cries out against you, accusing you and saying, "Their rage is like the serpent's"; but if you imitate its shrewdness, you become a disciple of Christ, who said, "Be shrewd as the serpent." For since the serpent is "shrewder than all the beasts," as was read just now, he set shrewdness against shrewdness. He did not do this so that you would learn to deceive, but so that you would learn to avoid deceit.

For the God who loves mankind wants us to be not malicious but cunning; and cunning is one thing, malice another. The cunning man uses his skill not to devise evil but to escape it. He uses his cunning not to scheme against others but to slip free of what others weave against him. The malicious man is the murderer, the deceiver, the one who contrives evil against others. Jacob was shrewd in this way: shrewd as the serpent, not venomous as the serpent. When he was about to meet his brother Esau, who was full of malice and murderous intent, he called on God, saying, "Lord, deliver me from my brother Esau, for I fear him greatly." He implored God as one setting his prayer against a wicked man. But when he met his brother, he tamed his anger with courtesy and flattery and quenched his wickedness. What does he say to Esau? "I have seen your face, as one might see the face of God." If Jacob said this in order to get the better of his brother by deceit, he spoke wrongly. But if he said it in order to escape the danger he feared, he used his cunning well. "Be," then, "shrewd as the serpent" – not wrathful, not venomous, but shrewd – "and innocent as the doves." The dove too can be taken either for vice or for virtue. Listen to how. If you are thoughtless and undiscerning, experienced only in vice, Scripture condemns you as senseless, for it says, "Ephraim is like a silly dove, without heart." But if you flee the senselessness and achieve the innocence, you have perfect understanding, not mixed with vice itself. And you hear from the Lord: "Be shrewd as the serpent and innocent as the doves." So do not read the Scriptures carelessly, brother, and take the images in them as referring to vices; Scripture assigns one meaning here and another there. Do you want to learn? Pay close attention to what is said. Scripture calls someone a lion: "Judah," it says, "is a lion's whelp; from a shoot, my son, you have gone up; you lay down and slept like a lion." Here "like a lion" signifies courage, for it uses the same image for the righteous man as well: "The righteous," it says, "is confident like a lion." The righteous man is courageous, then, not in doing harm but in scorning what the wicked bring against him. Scripture also calls the Saviour a lion because he is of a royal tribe. Just as the lion is king of the four-footed beasts, so the tribe of Judah, from which the Saviour rose, reigned over the Jews. And do not think, beloved, that it is unworthy of Christ to be likened to a lion. Scripture draws this image even for the Godhead itself. Listen to what the prophet says: "A lion will roar, and who will not fear? The Lord God has spoken, and who will not prophesy?" So Christ is likened to a lion in his power, his fearsomeness and his royalty. But the devil too is called a lion, not as powerful or as fearsome, but as violent, as a tyrant, as a destroyer. Of him the blessed apostle Peter says: "Behold, your enemy the devil prowls about like a lion, seeking to devour a soul." So distinguish the meanings of the readings, lest passages whose words seem to contradict each other confuse your mind. Scripture said "lion" and "lion," but meant the one for his royalty and power, the other for his destructiveness and harm. In the same way Scripture depicts both the righteous and the ungodly with a single image: "The righteous," it says, "will flourish like a palm tree; he will be multiplied like the cedar in Lebanon." First it drew the image of the righteous, then that of the ungodly as well: "I saw the ungodly," it says, "exalted and lifted up like the cedars of Lebanon." See, then, how it brought forward the same image but distinguished the meanings by its words. Of the ungodly it says, "I saw the ungodly exalted and lifted up like the cedars"; but of the righteous it did not say, "He will blossom like the cedar in Lebanon," but, "He will be multiplied." In the same way, O man, imitate the bee, which Scripture also teaches us to imitate for her industry: "Go to the bee and learn how hard she works." Do not learn from her that she has a sting, but that she makes honey. If you imitate the bee's sting, David accuses you, saying, "All the nations surrounded me like bees around a honeycomb, and in the name of the Lord I drove them back." Do you see how he likens those who strike to the stinging bee, but likens the righteous to the bee that drips honey? For "the lips of righteous men," it says, "drip wisdom, and good words are a honeycomb; and their sweetness is healing for the soul." So, beloved, let us long with all our soul for this sweetness of souls, I say. Let us make the spiritual honeycomb in the hidden workshop of the soul, and receive the divine oracles as "sweeter than honey and the honeycomb." Honey eaten in quantity often turns its sweetness to bitterness, spoils the stomach's appetite and upsets a person's whole constitution. But the word of God, taken in abundance, does not trouble the soul; it heals it, "for its sweetness is healing for the soul." That is why the wise man, wishing to set out the difference between honey and the word, says: "It is not good to eat much honey, but one must honour glorious words." So, beloved, let us always keep the many-patterned honeycomb, the divine and sacred oracles. That honeycomb is built from many different cells, yet it holds one good thing. So let the divine Scripture be a honeycomb for us: it is composed of many different prophets, yet it drips one honey of teaching. Such too for us is the honeycomb of the Fathers. It is put together from different ages, yet it drips one grace and one spiritual teaching. But enough of this.

By the prayers and intercessions of our common father, may we increase the word through diligence and always work out the divine law in our minds. May we do what David spoke of, keeping the law of God, that is, the divine thoughts, always in the depths of our inner being. So may we come to recognise [?] the bounds of nature, honour the truth, despise the world, and send up glory to God, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
